elements.text: The last study explained that we are saved when we put our faith in Jesus Christ and repent of our sins. But how can we be sure that it has really happened, and that it will last? A traveller with a valid ticket can board with confidence; one who is unsure may spend the whole journey worrying. In this study we look at what the Bible says about being certain that we truly are saved.
Why was the Bible written?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup>I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God so that you may know that you have eternal life.

elements.question: Why does John say he wrote his letter, and who is he writing to?
elements.sampleAnswer: John writes to those who believe in the name of the Son of God. His purpose is that they may know that they have eternal life. He does not want them merely to hope or to guess; he wants them to be sure. So certainty about salvation is something God wants believers to have, not something to be shy about.
elements.questionHint: Look at the word ‘know’: what is the difference between hoping you have eternal life and knowing you have it?

elements.question: Is it arrogant to be sure that you are saved?
elements.answer: Some people feel that being sure of salvation is presumptuous, as if they were claiming to be good enough. But the Bible says the opposite. In 1 John 5:13, John writes so that believers may know they have eternal life. Certainty does not rest on how well we are doing; it rests on what God has promised and what Christ has done. That is why the rest of this study keeps pointing to God’s promises rather than to our performance.

elements.text: What has Jesus Christ promised?

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup>Yet to all who did receive him, to those who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God –

elements.question: John says some people were given ‘the right to become children of God’. Who are they, and how did they respond to Jesus?
elements.sampleAnswer: The right is given to those who received Jesus and believed in his name. John describes one response in two ways: receiving him and believing in him. The right is something that was given, so it is a gift and not a reward. Anyone who has received and believed in Jesus is therefore a child of God.
elements.questionHint: Notice who gives the right: does that suggest it is something we earn or something we are given?

elements.passageText: <sup>47</sup>Very truly I tell you, the one who believes has eternal life.

elements.question: Jesus begins with ‘Very truly I tell you’. What does he say the one who believes has, and why might it matter that he says ‘has’ rather than ‘will have’?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus says that the one who believes has eternal life. He uses the present tense, so it is not only a hope for the future but something the believer already possesses. His opening words show he is making a solemn promise. That gives real confidence, because it rests on Jesus’ word rather than on how we feel on a particular day.
elements.questionHint: Which wording would give more confidence to someone who believes right now?

elements.passageText: <sup>27</sup>My sheep listen to my voice; I know them, and they follow me. <sup>28</sup>I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish; no one will snatch them out of my hand.

elements.question: Jesus describes his sheep and what he gives them. What does he promise about their future, and how does the picture of ‘my hand’ strengthen the promise?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus says he gives his sheep eternal life, that they will never perish, and that no one will snatch them out of his hand. The sheep listen to his voice and follow him, but the promise rests on what Jesus does: he gives and he holds. Their safety depends on his strength, not on their own grip. That is a firm basis for being certain about the future.
elements.questionHint: Think about who is doing the holding: if the sheep are in Jesus’ hand, who is responsible for keeping them safe?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup>Here I am! I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in and eat with that person, and they with me.

elements.question: In this verse, who takes the initiative, and what does Jesus ask a person to do? What does he promise if they respond?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus takes the initiative: he stands at the door and knocks. He asks the person who hears his voice to open the door. If they do, he promises to come in and eat with them, a picture of close friendship in which each shares with the other. The promise to come in is one a person can rely on once they have responded.
elements.questionHint: Notice where Jesus is standing and what he is doing: who is waiting for whom?

elements.text: How can we be sure that we truly are God’s children?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup>The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children.

elements.question: Who testifies that we are God’s children, and what does he testify with? What might this mean for a believer who feels unsure?
elements.sampleAnswer: The Spirit himself testifies, and he does so with our spirit, that is, he bears witness within the believer. What he testifies is that we are God’s children. For someone who feels unsure, this means certainty is not left to our own reasoning alone. God’s own Spirit assures believers that they belong to him.
elements.questionHint: The verse mentions two spirits: work out whose they are and what the one does with the other.

elements.text: How can we be certain that Jesus will always be with us?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup>And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.

elements.question: What does Jesus promise his disciples about his presence, and for how long does the promise last?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus promises that he is with his disciples always. No exceptions or conditions are mentioned, and the promise runs ‘to the very end of the age’. Believers are therefore never left to carry on alone, however hard things become. It is a reason to be certain that Jesus will not leave us.
elements.questionHint: Look at the last words of the verse: is there any limit on when Jesus will be with them?

elements.text: How can we be certain that we will be able to keep going as a Christian?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup>To him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you before his glorious presence without fault and with great joy –

elements.question: Jude begins with praise to ‘him who is able’. What is he able to do for believers, and what is the end result?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jude says God is able to keep believers from stumbling and to present them before his glorious presence without fault and with great joy. The focus is on what he is able to do, not on the believer’s own strength. That is why a Christian can be certain of keeping going: the one who keeps them is able to do it. The end result is joy, not fear.
elements.questionHint: Notice that the verse is praise addressed to God and describes what he is able to do: whose strength is the focus?

elements.passageText: <sup>31</sup>What, then, shall we say in response to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? <sup>32</sup>He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all – how will he not also, along with him, graciously give us all things? <sup>33</sup>Who will bring any charge against those whom God has chosen? It is God who justifies. <sup>34</sup>Who then is the one who condemns? No one. Christ Jesus who died – more than that, who was raised to life – is at the right hand of God and is also interceding for us. <sup>35</sup>Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or hardship or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword? <sup>36</sup>As it is written: ‘For your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.’ <sup>37</sup>No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. <sup>38</sup>For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, <sup>39</sup>neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

elements.question: In verses 31 to 34 Paul asks several questions. What reasons does he give for being sure that no one can successfully accuse or condemn God’s people?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that if God is for us, no one can be against us. God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, so he will graciously give us everything else. It is God who justifies, so no charge against his chosen people can stand. Christ Jesus, who died and was raised and is at God’s right hand interceding for us, is on our side, so no one can condemn us.
elements.questionHint: Look at who justifies, who died and was raised, and where Christ is now: what is each doing for believers?

elements.text: What can separate us from Christ’s love?

elements.question: Paul lists many things that might seem to threaten our relationship with God. Name some of them, and say what he concludes.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul names trouble, hardship, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger and sword, then death, life, angels, demons, the present, the future, powers, height, depth and anything else in creation. His conclusion is that none of these will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. In all these things believers are ‘more than conquerors’ through him who loved us. The certainty rests on the strength of Christ’s love, not on our circumstances.
elements.questionHint: Read verses 35, 38 and 39 together: he lists dangers in this life, things beyond it, and then adds a final catch-all.

elements.text: When we sin as Christians, what must we do? What does God promise?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup>If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness.

elements.question: What does John say we should do when we sin, what does he say God will do, and what does that show about God’s character?
elements.sampleAnswer: John says that if we confess our sins, God will forgive us and purify us from all unrighteousness. He describes God as faithful and just, so we can rely on him to keep this promise. Confession is the believer’s response when they sin, and forgiveness is God’s response. So when a Christian sins, the way back is open.
elements.questionHint: Look at the two words John uses to describe God: what do they tell you about whether he can be relied on to keep this promise?

elements.text: Key truths

Jesus will receive everyone whom the Father gives Him.

“All those the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never drive away.” — John 6:37

When we sin we do not lose our salvation but we do need to confess our sin to God: unconfessed sin clouds our relationship with Him.

“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
To think about

elements.question: Do you ever doubt whether you truly are a child of God? If so, how do you deal with those doubts?
John 6:37 speaks of the Father giving believers to Jesus. Do you thank God for that? How could it become a daily habit?

chapters.chapterTitle: The Cost of Living as a Christian

elements.text: Imagine being given a free place in a marathon. The place costs you nothing, but running the race will cost you plenty. Salvation is a free gift, and there is nothing we can do to earn it. Yet the Christian life is a real race, and following Jesus has a cost. In this study we look at what it means to be a Christian, what we must give up, what we take on, and the opposition we may face.
What does it mean to be a Christian?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, I urge you, brothers and sisters, in view of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God – this is your true and proper worship. <sup>2</sup>Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God’s will is – his good, pleasing and perfect will.

elements.question: Paul urges believers to offer something to God. What is it, and how does he describe it? What two commands does he give in verse 2, and what will follow?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul urges believers to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, and calls this their true and proper worship. In verse 2 he gives two commands: do not conform to the pattern of this world, and be transformed by the renewing of your mind. The result is that they will be able to test and approve what God’s will is. Being a Christian therefore involves the whole of a person’s life, not just part of it.
elements.questionHint: Notice that Paul begins ‘in view of God’s mercy’: what does that suggest about why believers respond in this way?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup>‘You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its saltiness, how can it be made salty again? It is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot. <sup>14</sup>‘You are the light of the world. A town built on a hill cannot be hidden. <sup>15</sup>Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a bowl. Instead they put it on its stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house. <sup>16</sup>In the same way, let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.

elements.question: Jesus uses two pictures to describe his followers. What are they, and what does each suggest about how a Christian is to affect the people around them?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus calls his followers the salt of the earth and the light of the world. Salt that loses its saltiness is good for nothing, and a light is not meant to be hidden under a bowl but placed where everyone can see it. Christians are therefore to be visibly different, for the benefit of others. Jesus says the purpose is that people may see their good deeds and glorify their Father in heaven.
elements.questionHint: Think about what salt and light each do to the thing they touch, and what would be lost if they were hidden or lost their effect.

elements.question: If salvation is a free gift, why does following Jesus cost anything?
elements.answer: Some people think that because salvation is free, the Christian life should cost nothing, or that what we give up is the price of being saved. Neither is right. Salvation is a gift that nothing we do can earn. The cost is the cost of discipleship: following Jesus changes how we live, what we give up and what we take on, and it can bring opposition. That is why Jesus says it is not a decision to be taken lightly.

elements.text: What must we give up if we are to follow Jesus Christ?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off everything that hinders and the sin that so easily entangles. And let us run with perseverance the race marked out for us,

elements.question: The writer uses the picture of a race. What two things must we throw off, and what are we to do instead?
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer says we must throw off everything that hinders and the sin that so easily entangles. These are named separately, so some things may slow us down even if they are not sinful in themselves. Instead we are to run with perseverance the race marked out for us. The picture of a great cloud of witnesses suggests we are not running alone.
elements.questionHint: Notice that the writer names ‘everything that hinders’ and ‘the sin that so easily entangles’ separately: what might be the difference between them?

elements.text: What are some of the specific things?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup>Put to death, therefore, whatever belongs to your earthly nature: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires and greed, which is idolatry. <sup>6</sup>Because of these, the wrath of God is coming. <sup>7</sup>You used to walk in these ways, in the life you once lived. <sup>8</sup>But now you must also rid yourselves of all such things as these: anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language from your lips. <sup>9</sup>Do not lie to each other, since you have taken off your old self with its practices <sup>10</sup>and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator. <sup>11</sup>Here there is no Gentile or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave or free, but Christ is all, and is in all.

elements.question: Paul lists things to put to death and things to get rid of. Make two lists from the passage. What reasons does he give for leaving them behind?
elements.sampleAnswer: The first list is sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires and greed, which Paul calls idolatry. The second is anger, rage, malice, slander and filthy language, with a command not to lie to each other. The reasons are that God’s wrath is coming because of these things, and that believers have taken off the old self and put on the new self, which is being renewed in the image of its Creator.
elements.questionHint: Paul gives one list in verse 5 and another in verse 8, and then explains in verses 9 and 10 what has already happened to believers.

elements.text: What are some of the new things we must take on as disciples of Jesus Christ?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Therefore if you have any encouragement from being united with Christ, if any comfort from his love, if any common sharing in the Spirit, if any tenderness and compassion, <sup>2</sup>then make my joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being one in spirit and of one mind. <sup>3</sup>Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit. Rather, in humility value others above yourselves, <sup>4</sup>not looking to your own interests but each of you to the interests of the others. <sup>5</sup>In your relationships with one another, have the same mindset as Christ Jesus:

elements.question: What attitudes does Paul say should mark Christians in their relationships with one another? What does he tell them to avoid, and whose example does he point to?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul asks believers to be like-minded, with the same love, one in spirit and of one mind. They are to do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility to value others above themselves. Each is to look to the interests of others, not only their own. He points to Christ Jesus, saying they should have the same mindset as he had.
elements.questionHint: Look at what Paul says to avoid in verse 3 and what he asks believers to do instead in verses 3 and 4.

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup>Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful.

elements.question: What does Paul ask Christians to devote themselves to, and what two attitudes should go with it?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul asks Christians to devote themselves to prayer. He adds two attitudes: being watchful and being thankful. Devotion suggests a regular, committed habit rather than something done only when it is convenient. Prayer is therefore one of the new things a disciple takes on.
elements.questionHint: Think about what it means to be ‘devoted’ to something rather than doing it now and then.

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup>And let us consider how we may spur one another on towards love and good deeds, <sup>25</sup>not giving up meeting together, as some are in the habit of doing, but encouraging one another – and all the more as you see the Day approaching.

elements.question: What does the writer say we should think about doing for one another, and what habit does he warn against? Why should we do this all the more?
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer says we should consider how to spur one another on towards love and good deeds. He warns against giving up meeting together, which some were in the habit of doing, and says instead we should encourage one another. We are to do this all the more as we see the Day approaching. Meeting with other Christians is therefore a way of helping one another keep going.
elements.questionHint: Look at what meeting together is meant to achieve, not only the fact of meeting.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>And now, brothers and sisters, we want you to know about the grace that God has given the Macedonian churches. <sup>2</sup>In the midst of a very severe trial, their overflowing joy and their extreme poverty welled up in rich generosity. <sup>3</sup>For I testify that they gave as much as they were able, and even beyond their ability. Entirely on their own, <sup>4</sup>they urgently pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the Lord’s people. <sup>5</sup>And they exceeded our expectations: they gave themselves first of all to the Lord, and then by the will of God also to us. <sup>6</sup>So we urged Titus, just as he had earlier made a beginning, to bring also to completion this act of grace on your part. <sup>7</sup>But since you excel in everything – in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in complete earnestness and in the love we have kindled in you – see that you also excel in this grace of giving.

<sup>6</sup>Remember this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously. <sup>7</sup>Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

elements.question: What do these passages tell us about how the Macedonian Christians gave, and about the attitude God looks for in giving?
elements.sampleAnswer: The Macedonians gave in the midst of a very severe trial and extreme poverty. Their overflowing joy led them to give as much as they were able, and even beyond, and they pleaded for the privilege of sharing, giving themselves first to the Lord. Paul says each person should give what they have decided in their heart to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver. Giving is therefore something a disciple takes on, from the heart.
elements.questionHint: Notice the circumstances of the Macedonians in 8:2: does generous giving depend on being comfortable?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup>Now the Berean Jews were of more noble character than those in Thessalonica, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if what Paul said was true.

elements.question: What did the Berean Jews do that led Luke to call them ‘of more noble character’? What was their attitude, and what was their habit?
elements.sampleAnswer: The Bereans received the message with great eagerness. They also examined the Scriptures every day to see whether what Paul said was true. Their attitude was eager and open, and their habit was regular study of the Bible. A disciple likewise takes on the habit of studying Scripture and checking what is taught against it.
elements.questionHint: Notice both how they received the message and what they did with it afterwards.

elements.text: What opposition did the early Christians face?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>The priests and the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees came up to Peter and John while they were speaking to the people. <sup>2</sup>They were greatly disturbed because the apostles were teaching the people, proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead. <sup>3</sup>They seized Peter and John and, because it was evening, they put them in jail until the next day. <sup>4</sup>But many who heard the message believed; so the number of men who believed grew to about five thousand. ... <sup>18</sup>Then they called them in again and commanded them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. <sup>19</sup>But Peter and John replied, ‘Which is right in God’s eyes: to listen to you, or to him? You be the judges! <sup>20</sup>As for us, we cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard.’ <sup>21</sup>After further threats they let them go. They could not decide how to punish them, because all the people were praising God for what had happened. <sup>22</sup>For the man who was miraculously healed was over forty years old.

<sup>17</sup>Then the high priest and all his associates, who were members of the party of the Sadducees, were filled with jealousy. <sup>18</sup>They arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail.

<sup>1</sup>And Saul approved of their killing him. On that day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered throughout Judea and Samaria. <sup>2</sup>Godly men buried Stephen and mourned deeply for him. <sup>3</sup>But Saul began to destroy the church. Going from house to house, he dragged off both men and women and put them in prison.

elements.question: What forms of opposition did the early Christians face in these passages? How did Peter and John respond?
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter and John were seized and put in jail, and then commanded not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. Later the apostles were arrested again because the high priest and his associates were filled with jealousy. After Stephen was killed a great persecution broke out, the believers were scattered, and Saul dragged men and women off to prison. Peter and John refused to be silenced, saying they could not help speaking about what they had seen and heard.
elements.questionHint: Look for what the authorities did in each passage, and then for what Peter and John said.

elements.text: What warning has Jesus given His disciples?

elements.passageText: <sup>33</sup>‘I have told you these things, so that in me you may have peace. In this world you will have trouble. But take heart! I have overcome the world.’

elements.question: What does Jesus warn his disciples to expect, and what does he give them to hold on to?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus warns that in this world his followers will have trouble. But he has told them this so that in him they may have peace, and he tells them to take heart because he has overcome the world. The warning is not meant to frighten them, since the victory is already his.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says why he has told them these things: look at the beginning and the end of the verse.

elements.text: How should we react if we suffer because of our faith?

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup>Dear friends, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal that has come on you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. <sup>13</sup>But rejoice inasmuch as you participate in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed when his glory is revealed. <sup>14</sup>If you are insulted because of the name of Christ, you are blessed, for the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you. <sup>15</sup>If you suffer, it should not be as a murderer or thief or any other kind of criminal, or even as a meddler. <sup>16</sup>However, if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but praise God that you bear that name.

elements.question: How does Peter say Christians should react when they suffer for their faith? What distinction does he make between different kinds of suffering?
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter says believers should not be surprised at the fiery ordeal, as though something strange were happening. Instead they should rejoice that they share in Christ’s sufferings, because they will be overjoyed when his glory is revealed. Those insulted because of Christ’s name are blessed, since the Spirit of glory rests on them. But suffering should not be as a criminal; if it is as a Christian, they should not be ashamed but should praise God.
elements.questionHint: Peter says what believers should not feel, what they should do instead, and which kind of suffering should never be deserved.

elements.text: Key truths

Following Jesus can be costly. It is not a decision to be taken lightly.

“‘If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters – yes, even their own life – such a person cannot be my disciple. And whoever does not carry their cross and follow me cannot be my disciple...’” — Luke 14:26-27

We should recognise the value of trials: they test and strengthen our faith.

“Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance.” — James 1:2-3
To think about

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>who, being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage; <sup>7</sup>rather, he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant, being made in human likeness. <sup>8</sup>And being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to death – even death on a cross!

elements.question: What has been most costly for you as a follower of Jesus?
How are Christians being persecuted in many countries today? Do you pray for them regularly?
Reflect again on what it cost Jesus to pay the penalty for our sins. What do these verses say he gave up and took on?

elements.text: A hiker on an unlit path at night is glad of a lamp. It will not show the whole journey, but it shows the next steps. Christians need to grow more like Jesus, and the Bible is our vital source of spiritual food. In this study we look at how important the Bible was to Jesus, why and how it was given to us, and how we should respond to it.
How do we know the Bible was important to Jesus?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, left the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, <sup>2</sup>where for forty days he was tempted by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and at the end of them he was hungry. <sup>3</sup>The devil said to him, ‘If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.’ <sup>4</sup>Jesus answered, ‘It is written: “Man shall not live on bread alone.”’ <sup>5</sup>The devil led him up to a high place and showed him in an instant all the kingdoms of the world. <sup>6</sup>And he said to him, ‘I will give you all their authority and splendour; it has been given to me, and I can give it to anyone I want to. <sup>7</sup>If you worship me, it will all be yours.’ <sup>8</sup>Jesus answered, ‘It is written: “Worship the Lord your God and serve him only.”’ <sup>9</sup>The devil led him to Jerusalem and had him stand on the highest point of the temple. ‘If you are the Son of God,’ he said, ‘throw yourself down from here. <sup>10</sup>For it is written: ‘“He will command his angels concerning you to guard you carefully; <sup>11</sup>they will lift you up in their hands, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone.”’ <sup>12</sup>Jesus answered, ‘It is said: “Do not put the Lord your God to the test.”’ <sup>13</sup>When the devil had finished all this tempting, he left him until an opportune time.

elements.question: How does Jesus answer each of the devil’s three temptations? What does this show about the place of Scripture in his life?
elements.sampleAnswer: To the first temptation Jesus answers that it is written that man shall not live on bread alone. To the second he answers that it is written, ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve him only.’ To the third he answers with a verse saying not to put the Lord your God to the test. Each time he answers from Scripture, so it must have been in his mind and he treated it as the final authority.
elements.questionHint: Look at how each of Jesus’ answers begins.

elements.text: Why was the Bible given to us?

elements.passageText: <sup>31</sup>But these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.

elements.question: Why does John say these things were written, and what result is intended for the reader?
elements.sampleAnswer: John says these things are written so that readers may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God. The second purpose is that by believing they may have life in his name. The aim is not only to give information but to lead people to faith in Jesus and so to life.
elements.questionHint: The verse gives two purposes joined by ‘and’: look for the belief and the life.

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup>and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. <sup>16</sup>All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, <sup>17</sup>so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.

elements.question: What can the Holy Scriptures do for a person, where does Paul say they come from, and what is the goal?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says the Scriptures are able to make a person wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is God-breathed, which means it comes from God. It is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness. The goal is that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.
elements.questionHint: Verse 15 says what Scripture can do for you, verse 16 gives its origin and four uses, and verse 17 gives the aim.

elements.text: How was the Bible given to us?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup>We also have the prophetic message as something completely reliable, and you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. <sup>20</sup>Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture came about by the prophet’s own interpretation of things. <sup>21</sup>For prophecy never had its origin in the human will, but prophets, though human, spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

elements.question: How does Peter say prophecy did not come about, and how did it? What roles do the human writers and the Holy Spirit play?
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter says prophecy never came about by the prophet’s own interpretation or from the human will. Instead, prophets, though human, spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. So real people wrote, but the message came from God through the Holy Spirit. That is why Peter calls it completely reliable and worth paying attention to.
elements.questionHint: Notice what Peter says does not account for prophecy before he says what does.

elements.question: What do you think people mean when they say the Bible is ‘inspired’?
elements.answer: In everyday speech, ‘inspired’ can mean a person had a brilliant idea, as with a great poem or a work of art. The Bible’s claim is stronger. It says that Scripture is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16) and that the prophets spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21). Human writers were really involved, but the Bible is not just a collection of human thoughts and ideas: God himself inspired and directed the writing to record what he wants us to know.

elements.text: In the Apostle Paul’s day, why and how did the Berean Jews study the Scriptures?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup>Now the Berean Jews were of more noble character than those in Thessalonica, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if what Paul said was true.

elements.question: Why did the Bereans examine the Scriptures, and how did they go about it?
elements.sampleAnswer: The Bereans received Paul’s message with great eagerness. They examined the Scriptures every day to see if what Paul said was true. Their purpose was to test the message against Scripture, not simply to accept it. Luke calls them of more noble character for doing so.
elements.questionHint: Look at their attitude, how often they studied, and what they were checking.

elements.text: With what result?

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup>As a result, many of them believed, as did also a number of prominent Greek women and many Greek men.

elements.question: What was the result of the Bereans’ study?
elements.sampleAnswer: Many of the Bereans believed. So did a number of prominent Greek women and many Greek men. Careful study of the Scriptures led to faith in Jesus.
elements.questionHint: Look at the opening words of the verse: ‘As a result’.

elements.text: What should we expect from God’s Word?

elements.passageText: <sup>105</sup>Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.

elements.question: What picture does the psalmist use for God’s word, and what does a lamp do for someone walking?
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist says God’s word is a lamp for his feet and a light on his path. A lamp shows the way ahead so that a traveller can walk without stumbling. In the same way, God’s word guides us in our decisions and direction day by day.
elements.questionHint: Think about what a light on a dark path lets a traveller see and do.

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup>When your words came, I ate them; they were my joy and my heart’s delight, for I bear your name, Lord God Almighty.

elements.question: What picture does Jeremiah use for receiving God’s words, what did they become for him, and what reason does he give?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jeremiah says that when God’s words came, he ate them, a picture of taking them in and being fed by them. They became his joy and his heart’s delight. He gives as his reason that he bears God’s name, as one who belongs to the Lord God Almighty. We can therefore expect God’s word to feed us and to bring real joy.
elements.questionHint: Notice the picture Jeremiah uses for taking in God’s words, and the reason he gives at the end of the verse.

elements.text: How should we respond to God’s Word?

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup>Do not merely listen to the word, and so deceive yourselves. Do what it says. <sup>23</sup>Anyone who listens to the word but does not do what it says is like someone who looks at his face in a mirror <sup>24</sup>and, after looking at himself, goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like. <sup>25</sup>But whoever looks intently into the perfect law that gives freedom and continues in it – not forgetting what they have heard but doing it – they will be blessed in what they do.

elements.question: What mistake does James warn against, and what picture does he use? What does the person who is blessed do?
elements.sampleAnswer: James warns against merely listening to the word, which deceives us. We must do what it says. He compares the one who only listens to someone who looks at his face in a mirror and then forgets what he looks like. The person who is blessed looks intently into the perfect law that gives freedom and continues in it, not forgetting but doing.
elements.questionHint: Compare the person who looks in the mirror and walks away with the one who ‘continues’ in the word.

elements.passageText: <sup>32</sup>‘Now I commit you to God and to the word of his grace, which can build you up and give you an inheritance among all those who are sanctified.

elements.question: What does Paul commit the Ephesian elders to, and what does he say God’s word can do?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul commits them to God and to the word of his grace. He says that word can build them up and give them an inheritance among all who are sanctified. God’s word therefore strengthens believers now and points them to what God has in store.
elements.questionHint: Look for the two things Paul commits them to, and for what the word is able to do for them.

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup>I have hidden your word in my heart that I might not sin against you.

elements.question: What has the psalmist done with God’s word, and why?
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist says he has hidden God’s word in his heart. His reason is that he might not sin against God. Keeping God’s word in the heart gives a resource against temptation, which echoes how Jesus used Scripture in Luke 4.
elements.questionHint: Notice the purpose clause at the end of the verse.

elements.text: Key truths

Scripture is not just a collection of man’s random thoughts and ideas. God Himself inspired and directed the writing of it to record what He wants us to know.

“All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness,...” — 2 Timothy 3:16

The Bible is the Christian’s handbook for daily living: we cannot afford to neglect it.

“Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path. I have taken an oath and confirmed it, that I will follow your righteous laws.” — Psalm 119:105-106
To think about

elements.question: What priority do you give to regular reading of the Bible? If you are finding it difficult, what might you be able to do to fit this into your daily schedule?
Do you read the Bible expecting God to speak to you? Can you think of a time when He has clearly spoken to you?

elements.text: Imagine a friendship in which one person never speaks to the other. It would not stay close for long. Prayer is how we keep up a conversation with God, our Father: speaking to him and listening. We cannot keep a strong relationship with him without it. In this study we look at Jesus’ example, what prayer involves, and what the Bible tells us about praying.
How do we know that prayer was important to Jesus when He was on earth?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup>After he had dismissed them, he went up on a mountainside by himself to pray. Later that night, he was there alone,
<sup>35</sup>Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up, left the house and went off to a solitary place, where he prayed.
<sup>12</sup>One of those days Jesus went out to a mountainside to pray, and spent the night praying to God.

elements.question: What do these three passages tell us about when and where Jesus prayed, and how long he prayed?
elements.sampleAnswer: In Matthew he went up a mountainside by himself to pray and was still there alone late that night. In Mark he got up very early, while it was still dark, and went to a solitary place to pray. In Luke he went out to a mountainside and spent the night praying to God. Jesus made time for prayer, often alone and sometimes for a long time.
elements.questionHint: Look for the time of day, the setting and the length of time in each passage.

elements.text: What should prayer involve?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup>Then I acknowledged my sin to you and did not cover up my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the Lord.’ And you forgave the guilt of my sin.

elements.question: What does the psalmist do about his sin, and how does God respond?
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist acknowledges his sin and does not cover up his iniquity. He decides to confess his transgressions to the Lord. God responds by forgiving the guilt of his sin. So honest confession is part of prayer, and forgiveness follows.
elements.questionHint: Notice the things the psalmist says he did, and the one thing God did.

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. <sup>7</sup>And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

elements.question: What does Paul say we should do instead of being anxious, and what does he promise?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says not to be anxious about anything. In every situation we are to present our requests to God by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving. He promises that the peace of God, which goes beyond all understanding, will guard our hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.
elements.questionHint: Notice the different ways of praying Paul names: prayer, petition, thanksgiving and requests.

elements.passageText: <sup>30</sup>I urge you, brothers and sisters, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to join me in my struggle by praying to God for me.

<sup>9</sup>For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you. We continually ask God to fill you with the knowledge of his will through all the wisdom and understanding that the Spirit gives,

<sup>16</sup>I have not stopped giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers. <sup>17</sup>I keep asking that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, so that you may know him better.

elements.question: What does Paul ask the Romans to do for him, and what does he say he does for the Colossians and the Ephesians?
elements.sampleAnswer: In Romans Paul urges the believers to join in his struggle by praying to God for him. In Colossians he says he has not stopped praying for them, asking God to fill them with the knowledge of his will. In Ephesians he gives thanks for them and asks that God would give them the Spirit of wisdom and revelation so that they may know him better. So prayer includes praying for others and asking others to pray for us.
elements.questionHint: Look at who is praying for whom in each verse.

elements.question: When you think of prayer, what do you usually do?
elements.answer: Many people think of prayer mainly as asking God for things. The passages in this study show something wider. Prayer includes confessing our sins (Psalm 32:5), bringing our requests with thanksgiving (Philippians 4:6), praying for other people and asking them to pray for us. It is the conversation with our Father that the study begins with: speaking to him and listening.

elements.text: What instructions are given about praying?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>But when you pray, go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen. Then your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.

elements.question: Where does Jesus say we should pray, and what does he promise?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus says to go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen. He promises that the Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you. Prayer is therefore a private time with God.
elements.questionHint: Notice who sees what is done in secret, and who rewards.

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup>Let us then approach God’s throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.

elements.question: How are we told to approach God, and what will we receive?
elements.sampleAnswer: We are told to approach God’s throne of grace with confidence. Our need is met there, because we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need. We can therefore come expecting help rather than fearing rejection.
elements.questionHint: Notice the attitude we are to bring and the kind of throne we are approaching.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus told his disciples a parable to show them that they should always pray and not give up. <sup>2</sup>He said: ‘In a certain town there was a judge who neither feared God nor cared what people thought. <sup>3</sup>And there was a widow in that town who kept coming to him with the plea, “Grant me justice against my adversary.” <sup>4</sup>‘For some time he refused. But finally he said to himself, “Even though I don’t fear God or care what people think, <sup>5</sup>yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will see that she gets justice, so that she won’t eventually come and attack me!”’ <sup>6</sup>And the Lord said, ‘Listen to what the unjust judge says. <sup>7</sup>And will not God bring about justice for his chosen ones, who cry out to him day and night? Will he keep putting them off? <sup>8</sup>I tell you, he will see that they get justice, and quickly. However, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?’
<sup>17</sup>pray continually,

elements.question: Why does Jesus tell the parable of the widow and the judge, and what does the parable teach? What does Paul’s short instruction add?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus tells the parable to show his disciples that they should always pray and not give up. The widow keeps coming to the judge until he gives her justice, even though he cares nothing for God or people. Jesus says God will see that justice is done for his chosen ones who cry out to him day and night, and quickly. Paul’s instruction to pray continually adds that prayer is not an occasional activity but a constant habit.
elements.questionHint: The first verse of the parable gives Luke’s own explanation of its point.

elements.text: What can we learn from the prayers the Apostle Paul prayed for other Christians?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup>I keep asking that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, so that you may know him better.

<sup>9</sup>For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you. We continually ask God to fill you with the knowledge of his will through all the wisdom and understanding that the Spirit gives, <sup>10</sup>so that you may live a life worthy of the Lord and please him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God,

<sup>9</sup>And this is my prayer: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight, <sup>10</sup>so that you may be able to discern what is best and may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, <sup>11</sup>filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ – to the glory and praise of God.

elements.question: What does Paul ask God to do for these Christians? What do the requests have in common?
elements.sampleAnswer: In Ephesians he asks that they will be given the Spirit of wisdom and revelation so that they may know God better. In Colossians he asks that they be filled with the knowledge of God’s will so that they live a life worthy of the Lord, bearing fruit and growing in the knowledge of God. In Philippians he asks that their love will abound in knowledge and insight, so that they are pure and blameless and filled with the fruit of righteousness. The requests are mainly about knowing God better and living well, rather than about comfort or circumstances.
elements.questionHint: Look for words such as knowledge, wisdom, love and fruit.

elements.text: Why might God not answer our prayers as we would wish?

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup>or because of these surpassingly great revelations. Therefore, in order to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me. <sup>8</sup>Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me. <sup>9</sup>But he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Therefore I will boast all the more gladly about my weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may rest on me.

elements.question: What did Paul ask the Lord for, how often did he ask, and how did the Lord answer? What did Paul conclude?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul pleaded three times for the Lord to take away the thorn in his flesh. The Lord did not remove it but said that his grace was sufficient and that his power is made perfect in weakness. Paul concluded that he would boast all the more gladly about his weaknesses so that Christ’s power might rest on him. God may answer in a different way from the one we ask for.
elements.questionHint: Notice that the Lord does respond, but not in the way Paul asked.

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup>When you ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may spend what you get on your pleasures.

elements.question: What reason does James give for asking and not receiving?
elements.sampleAnswer: James says we do not receive because we ask with wrong motives. Specifically, we want to spend what we get on our own pleasures. Selfish motives are therefore one reason prayers may go unanswered, different from the reason in 2 Corinthians 12.
elements.questionHint: Look at the words ‘wrong motives’ and what the person plans to do with what they receive.

elements.text: How does the Holy Spirit help us to pray?

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup>In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans.

elements.question: What does the Spirit do for us in prayer, and what problem does this help with?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says the Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans. So even when we do not know what to say, we are not left without help in prayer.
elements.questionHint: Notice what Paul says we do not know and what the Spirit does about it.

elements.text: Key truths

God longs that we spend time alone with Him.

“But when you pray, go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen. Then your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.” — Matthew 6:6

We can be sure of God’s grace and mercy in our times of need.

“Let us then approach God’s throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.” — Hebrews 4:16
To think about

elements.question: What have you learned from this study which might help you in your prayer life?
Do you already meet with other Christians to pray, either in a church setting or with just one or two friends? If not, perhaps it is something you might begin to do.

elements.text: Ask someone where the church is and they may point to a building on the corner. But the Bible uses the word ‘church’ to mean people, not a building: all who have put their trust in Jesus Christ. The word itself means a congregation, an assembly or a gathering, and the Christian Church is made up of all true believers, found in churches across the world. In this study we look at how the Church is described, who leads it, what it is for, and how its members belong together.
How is the Church described?

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup>Just as a body, though one, has many parts, but all its many parts form one body, so it is with Christ. ... <sup>27</sup>Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it.

elements.question: What picture does Paul use for the church, and how does it describe the relationship between Christ, the church and each believer?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul compares the church to a body that has many parts but is one body. He says this is how it is with Christ, and then tells his readers that they are the body of Christ and that each of them is a part of it. The church is therefore one united body that belongs to Christ, and every believer has a place in it.
elements.questionHint: Notice that Paul says ‘so it is with Christ’ and then speaks directly to his readers as ‘a part’.

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup>Consequently, you are no longer foreigners and strangers, but fellow citizens with God’s people and also members of his household, <sup>20</sup>built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone.

elements.question: How does Paul describe the people who now belong to God’s people, and what is the church built on?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says they are no longer foreigners and strangers but fellow citizens with God’s people and members of his household. The church is also like a building. It is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone.
elements.questionHint: Look at what these Christians used to be and what they are now, and then at the building picture in verse 20.

elements.question: When someone says ‘the church’, what do you usually picture?
elements.answer: In everyday speech, ‘church’ often means a building, a service or a particular denomination. In the Bible the word means people. It means a congregation, an assembly or a gathering: everyone who has put their trust in Jesus Christ. That is why Paul can call the church a body, a household and God’s people, and why the Church is found in churches across the world rather than in one place.

elements.passageText: <sup>25</sup>Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her <sup>26</sup>to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, <sup>27</sup>and to present her to himself as a radiant church, without stain or wrinkle or any other blemish, but holy and blameless.

elements.question: What did Christ do for the church, and what is his purpose for her?
elements.sampleAnswer: Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. His purpose was to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word. He wants to present her to himself as a radiant church, without stain or wrinkle or any other blemish, but holy and blameless. The church belongs to Christ, who loved her at great cost.
elements.questionHint: Look at the verbs Paul uses for what Christ did, and then at the words describing the church he wants to present to himself.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup>But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s special possession, that you may declare the praises of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light. <sup>10</sup>Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.

elements.question: What descriptions does Peter give of God’s people, and what has changed for them?
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter calls them a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation and God’s special possession. He then contrasts what they were with what they are now. Once they were not a people, but now they are the people of God. Once they had not received mercy, but now they have.
elements.questionHint: Count the descriptions in verse 9, and notice the ‘once … now’ contrast in verse 10.

elements.text: Who is the head of the Church?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup>For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, his body, of which he is the Saviour.

elements.question: Who does Paul say is the head of the church, and what does he call the church and Christ in relation to it?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that Christ is the head of the church. The church is his body, and Christ is its Saviour. So the church does not belong to any human leader but to Christ.
elements.questionHint: Look for the comparison Paul makes and the two descriptions given in the second half of the verse.

elements.text: What is the purpose of the Church?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup>But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

elements.question: What will the disciples receive, what will they be, and where will their witness spread?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus says the disciples will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on them. They will then be his witnesses, starting in Jerusalem and spreading to all Judea and Samaria and to the ends of the earth. The purpose of the church is therefore to take the message about Jesus out from where it is to the whole world.
elements.questionHint: Follow the widening circle of places Jesus names.

elements.question: In 1 Peter 2:9, God’s people are described as chosen ‘that you may …’. What purpose does Peter give, and what does it say about where they have been called from?
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter says they are chosen that they may declare the praises of him who called them out of darkness into his wonderful light. Their purpose is to speak about God’s goodness to others. This fits the picture in Acts 1:8 of a church that bears witness to Jesus.
elements.questionHint: Look for the words ‘that you may’ in verse 9.

elements.text: Why should Christians meet together (as a local church)?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup>He went to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and on the Sabbath day he went into the synagogue, as was his custom. He stood up to read,
<sup>42</sup>They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.

elements.question: What do these verses show about the habits of Jesus and of the first Christians when it came to meeting together? What did the first believers devote themselves to?
elements.sampleAnswer: Luke says Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, as was his custom. The first believers devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. Meeting together regularly was normal for Jesus and for the earliest Christians.
elements.questionHint: Look for the phrase ‘as was his custom’ and the four things listed in Acts 2:42.

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup>And let us consider how we may spur one another on towards love and good deeds, <sup>25</sup>not giving up meeting together, as some are in the habit of doing, but encouraging one another – and all the more as you see the Day approaching.

elements.question: What does the writer say meeting together is for, and what makes it all the more important?
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer says we should consider how we may spur one another on towards love and good deeds. Meeting together is a way of encouraging one another, and we are not to give it up as some have. It becomes all the more important as the Day approaches.
elements.questionHint: Look at what we are to consider doing for one another and at the reason given at the end of the passage.

elements.text: What is God’s desire for us as believers together?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Brothers and sisters, if someone is caught in a sin, you who live by the Spirit should restore that person gently. But watch yourselves, or you also may be tempted. <sup>2</sup>Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfil the law of Christ.

elements.question: What does Paul tell believers to do for someone caught in sin, and in what way? What warning and what instruction follow?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says those who live by the Spirit should restore the person gently. They must also watch themselves, because they too may be tempted. He then tells them to carry each other’s burdens, and says that in this way they will fulfil the law of Christ.
elements.questionHint: Notice the word ‘gently’ and the warning that comes straight after it.

elements.passageText: <sup>21</sup>The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I don’t need you!’ And the head cannot say to the feet, ‘I don’t need you!’ <sup>22</sup>On the contrary, those parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, <sup>23</sup>and the parts that we think are less honourable we treat with special honour. And the parts that are unpresentable are treated with special modesty, <sup>24</sup>while our presentable parts need no special treatment. But God has put the body together, giving greater honour to the parts that lacked it, <sup>25</sup>so that there should be no division in the body, but that its parts should have equal concern for each other. <sup>26</sup>If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honoured, every part rejoices with it. <sup>27</sup>Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it.

elements.question: What does Paul say about how the parts of the body should treat one another? What happens when one part suffers or is honoured?
elements.sampleAnswer: No part can say to another, ‘I don’t need you.’ The parts that seem weaker are indispensable, and God has given greater honour to the parts that lacked it, so that there should be no division and each part should have equal concern for the others. If one part suffers, every part suffers with it, and if one is honoured, every part rejoices.
elements.questionHint: Look at what the eye and the head cannot say, and at what happens in verse 26.

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup>Then we will no longer be infants, tossed back and forth by the waves, and blown here and there by every wind of teaching and by the cunning and craftiness of people in their deceitful scheming. <sup>15</sup>Instead, speaking the truth in love, we will grow to become in every respect the mature body of him who is the head, that is, Christ. <sup>16</sup>From him the whole body, joined and held together by every supporting ligament, grows and builds itself up in love, as each part does its work.

elements.question: What does Paul say believers should no longer be, and what should they do instead? What does each part contribute to the growth of the body?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says believers should no longer be infants, tossed about and blown here and there by every wind of teaching. Instead, speaking the truth in love, they are to grow in every respect into Christ, who is the head. From him the whole body is joined and held together, and it builds itself up in love as each part does its work.
elements.questionHint: Compare the ‘infants’ of verse 14 with the ‘mature body’ of verse 15.

elements.text: Key truths

All Christians are part of one body, of which Christ is the head.

“From him the whole body, joined and held together by every supporting ligament, grows and builds itself up in love, as each part does its work.” — Ephesians 4:16

The purpose of the Church is to take the message of Jesus Christ across the world (including our local communities).

“‘...But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.’” — Acts 1:8
To think about

elements.question: Are you helping your local church to fulfil its purpose? How?
How might you spur on others in your church ‘towards love and good deeds’ and encourage them? See Hebrews 10:24-25.

elements.text: When we hear the word ‘worship’, many of us think of singing. Music can certainly express our devotion, but worship is more than that. We worship God as we show our love, devotion and obedience to him in response to his grace, mercy and love, and that is the surrender of our whole lives, leading to obedient and willing service. In this study we look at what true worship is, the attitude in which we serve, and how we can worship and serve God in daily life, at work and by witnessing.
What is true worship?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, I urge you, brothers and sisters, in view of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God – this is your true and proper worship. <sup>2</sup>Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God’s will is – his good, pleasing and perfect will.

elements.question: What does Paul call ‘your true and proper worship’, and what does that suggest about how much of life worship covers?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul calls the offering of our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, our true and proper worship. Our bodies means the whole of our lives, not just a part of them. So worship is not limited to singing or to what happens at a service. It also involves not conforming to the pattern of this world but being transformed.
elements.questionHint: Notice how much of a person Paul asks to be offered to God.

elements.question: When you hear the word ‘worship’, what do you think of first?
elements.answer: Many people think of worship as the music at a church service. Music can be a good way to express devotion, but the Bible shows worship as something wider. It is the surrender of our whole lives to God (Romans 12:1), which then leads to obedient and willing service. So a Christian can worship God at home, at work, at school or university, and with friends, as well as in a meeting with other Christians.

elements.text: With what attitude did Jesus serve?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>It was just before the Passover Festival. Jesus knew that the hour had come for him to leave this world and go to the Father. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. <sup>2</sup>The evening meal was in progress, and the devil had already prompted Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, to betray Jesus. <sup>3</sup>Jesus knew that the Father had put all things under his power, and that he had come from God and was returning to God; <sup>4</sup>so he got up from the meal, took off his outer clothing, and wrapped a towel round his waist. <sup>5</sup>After that, he poured water into a basin and began to wash his disciples’ feet, drying them with the towel that was wrapped round him. <sup>6</sup>He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, ‘Lord, are you going to wash my feet?’ <sup>7</sup>Jesus replied, ‘You do not realise now what I am doing, but later you will understand.’ <sup>8</sup>‘No,’ said Peter, ‘you shall never wash my feet.’ Jesus answered, ‘Unless I wash you, you have no part with me.’ <sup>9</sup>‘Then, Lord,’ Simon Peter replied, ‘not just my feet but my hands and my head as well!’ <sup>10</sup>Jesus answered, ‘Those who have had a bath need only to wash their feet; their whole body is clean. And you are clean, though not every one of you.’ <sup>11</sup>For he knew who was going to betray him, and that was why he said not every one was clean. <sup>12</sup>When he had finished washing their feet, he put on his clothes and returned to his place. ‘Do you understand what I have done for you?’ he asked them. <sup>13</sup>‘You call me “Teacher” and “Lord”, and rightly so, for that is what I am. <sup>14</sup>Now that I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet. <sup>15</sup>I have set you an example that you should do as I have done for you. <sup>16</sup>Very truly I tell you, no servant is greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.

elements.question: What does Jesus do for his disciples, and what does it show about his attitude? What does he tell them to do as a result?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus knew that the Father had put all things under his power, yet he took off his outer clothing, wrapped a towel round his waist and washed his disciples’ feet. This shows a humble and loving attitude of service, since he had loved his own to the end. He tells them that he has set an example and that they should do as he has done for them, washing one another’s feet. No servant is greater than his master.
elements.questionHint: Look at what Jesus knew in verse 3 and then at what he did in verses 4 and 5.

elements.text: With what attitude should we express our worship as we serve God?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup>Enter his gates with thanksgiving and his courts with praise; give thanks to him and praise his name.

elements.question: What attitude and actions does the psalmist urge as we come to God?
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist says we should enter God’s gates with thanksgiving and his courts with praise. We are to give thanks to him and praise his name. Worship that serves God therefore begins with a grateful and praising attitude.
elements.questionHint: Look for the two things we are told to come with and what we are to give.

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup>Yet a time is coming and has now come when the true worshippers will worship the Father in the Spirit and in truth, for they are the kind of worshippers the Father seeks. <sup>24</sup>God is spirit, and his worshippers must worship in the Spirit and in truth.

elements.question: What kind of worshippers does Jesus say the Father seeks, and what does he say about God?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus says the true worshippers will worship the Father in the Spirit and in truth, and that these are the kind of worshippers the Father seeks. He explains that God is spirit, and so his worshippers must worship in the Spirit and in truth. True worship is therefore genuine and spiritual, not just an outward form.
elements.questionHint: Notice the two words that come after ‘in the Spirit and …’.

elements.text: What should be our attitude towards others?

elements.passageText: <sup>34</sup>‘A new command I give you: love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another. <sup>35</sup>By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.’
<sup>10</sup>Therefore, as we have opportunity, let us do good to all people, especially to those who belong to the family of believers.

elements.question: What new command does Jesus give, and what will it show the world? What does Paul add about doing good?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus gives a new command: love one another, as he has loved us. By this everyone will know that we are his disciples. Paul adds that as we have opportunity we should do good to all people, and especially to the family of believers.
elements.questionHint: Look at the standard Jesus sets with the words ‘As I have loved you’.

elements.text: How can we worship and serve God at work?

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup>Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything; and do it, not only when their eye is on you and to curry their favour, but with sincerity of heart and reverence for the Lord. <sup>23</sup>Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters, <sup>24</sup>since you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as a reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving. <sup>25</sup>Anyone who does wrong will be repaid for their wrongs, and there is no favouritism.

<sup>9</sup>Teach slaves to be subject to their masters in everything, to try to please them, not to talk back to them, <sup>10</sup>and not to steal from them, but to show that they can be fully trusted, so that in every way they will make the teaching about God our Saviour attractive.

elements.question: These words were written to slaves in the Roman world. What attitude and motive does Paul ask for in how they worked, and whom are they really serving?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul asks them to work with sincerity of heart and reverence for the Lord, and not only when someone is watching. They are to work at it with all their heart as working for the Lord, not for human masters. He reminds them that they will receive an inheritance from the Lord as a reward and that it is the Lord Christ they are serving. In Titus he adds that they should be fully trusted, so that the teaching about God is made attractive.
elements.questionHint: Look at the contrast between ‘human masters’ and ‘the Lord’ and at the reasons Paul gives for working well.

elements.text: Why should we serve Christ by witnessing?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup>Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, <sup>20</sup>and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.

elements.question: What command does Jesus give, and who is it for? What promise goes with it?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus tells his followers to go and make disciples of all nations. They are to baptise them in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and teach them to obey everything he has commanded. The promise is that he is with them always, to the very end of the age.
elements.questionHint: Count the things Jesus tells his followers to do in these two verses.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup>The Lord is not slow in keeping his promise, as some understand slowness. Instead he is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance.

elements.question: Why does Peter say the Lord has not yet acted, and what does God want for people?
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter says the Lord is not slow in keeping his promise, as some understand slowness. Instead he is patient, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance. God’s patience gives time for people to turn to him, which is a reason for us to tell them.
elements.questionHint: Look at how Peter describes the Lord when some think he is slow.

elements.text: How should we witness?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup>‘You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its saltiness, how can it be made salty again? It is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot. <sup>14</sup>‘You are the light of the world. A town built on a hill cannot be hidden. <sup>15</sup>Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a bowl. Instead they put it on its stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house. <sup>16</sup>In the same way, let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.

elements.question: What does Jesus say a light is for, and what should others see when it shines?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus says a lamp is not hidden under a bowl but put on its stand, where it gives light to everyone in the house. In the same way his followers are to let their light shine before others. People will then see their good deeds and give glory to their Father in heaven.
elements.questionHint: Look at where a lamp is put and why.

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup>Jesus did not let him, but said, ‘Go home to your own people and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.’ <sup>20</sup>So the man went away and began to tell in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him. And all the people were amazed.

elements.question: What does Jesus tell the man to do, and what did he do? What was the effect?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus tells the man to go home to his own people and tell them how much the Lord has done for him and how he has had mercy on him. The man went away and began to tell people in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him. All the people were amazed. Witnessing can be as simple as telling others what Jesus has done for us.
elements.questionHint: Notice where Jesus sends him and what he is told to say.

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup>But in your hearts revere Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have. But do this with gentleness and respect,

elements.question: What should be at the centre of a Christian’s heart, what should they always be ready to do, and in what manner?
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter says that in our hearts we should revere Christ as Lord. We should always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks for the reason for the hope we have. We are to do this with gentleness and respect.
elements.questionHint: Look for the instructions about the heart, about being ready, and about the manner.

elements.text: Key truths

We truly worship God when we surrender ourselves wholly and willingly to Him.

“Therefore, I urge you, brothers and sisters, in view of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God – this is your true and proper worship.” — Romans 12:1

We must follow Jesus’ supreme example in serving others.
