“‘...Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.’” — Mark 10:43-45
To think about

elements.passageText: <sup>38</sup>As Jesus and his disciples were on their way, he came to a village where a woman named Martha opened her home to him. <sup>39</sup>She had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet listening to what he said. <sup>40</sup>But Martha was distracted by all the preparations that had to be made. She came to him and asked, ‘Lord, don’t you care that my sister has left me to do the work by myself? Tell her to help me!’ <sup>41</sup>‘Martha, Martha,’ the Lord answered, ‘you are worried and upset about many things, <sup>42</sup>but few things are needed – or indeed only one. Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken away from her.’

elements.question: Where do you find it most difficult to worship (and serve) God? For example, in your home, in your workplace (or school or university), or socially with friends.
Do you ever serve out of a sense of duty, rather than willingly as an act of worship?
Read the account of Jesus in the home of Mary and Martha. What do you think of Martha’s complaint against her sister? What do you think of Jesus’ response?

elements.text: Many people picture the devil as a cartoon creature with cloven feet, horns and a tail, something of a joke. The truth is that he was once a heavenly being of great power and beauty. Pride and ambition brought about his fall, and he became the enemy of God and humanity. In this study we look at how Satan is described, how Jesus defeated him, how he attacks believers and unbelievers, how Christians should respond, and what will happen to him in the end.
How is Satan described?

elements.passageText: <sup>44</sup>You belong to your father, the devil, and you want to carry out your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, not holding to the truth, for there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks his native language, for he is a liar and the father of lies.

elements.question: What does Jesus say about the devil’s character and what he has done from the beginning?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus says the devil was a murderer from the beginning. He does not hold to the truth, and there is no truth in him. When he lies he speaks his native language, because he is a liar and the father of lies. Those who belong to him want to carry out his desires.
elements.questionHint: Look for the words Jesus uses for what the devil is and for what he does with the truth.

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup>And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light. <sup>15</sup>It is not surprising, then, if his servants also masquerade as servants of righteousness. Their end will be what their actions deserve.

elements.question: How does Paul say Satan disguises himself, and what does that suggest about his servants?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light. His servants likewise masquerade as servants of righteousness. This means that evil can look attractive and good. Paul adds that their end will be what their actions deserve.
elements.questionHint: Consider what ‘masquerades’ tells you about how evil may appear.

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup>when anyone hears the message about the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in their heart. This is the seed sown along the path.

elements.question: What does the evil one do when someone hears the message about the kingdom and does not understand it?
elements.sampleAnswer: The evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in the person’s heart. Jesus says this is the seed sown along the path. Satan tries to take the message before it can take root.
elements.questionHint: Think about what ‘snatches away’ suggests about how quickly this can happen.

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup>Be alert and of sober mind. Your enemy the devil prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour.

elements.question: What picture does Peter use for the devil, and what does he tell believers to be?
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter calls the devil our enemy and compares him to a roaring lion that prowls around looking for someone to devour. He tells believers to be alert and of sober mind. The devil is a real and dangerous enemy and is to be taken seriously.
elements.questionHint: Notice the two commands at the start of the verse and the image that follows.

elements.question: What picture of the devil do you have in mind?
elements.answer: Many people imagine a cartoon figure with horns and a tail, and so do not take him seriously. The Bible’s picture is quite different. The devil is a real and active enemy, a liar and a murderer who can disguise himself as an angel of light and prowls like a lion looking for someone to devour. At the same time, the Bible shows that Jesus has defeated him and that his end is certain, which is why Christians are told to resist him and stand firm.

elements.text: How did Jesus defeat Satan?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>As for you, you were dead in your transgressions and sins, <sup>2</sup>in which you used to live when you followed the ways of this world and of the ruler of the kingdom of the air, the spirit who is now at work in those who are disobedient. <sup>3</sup>All of us also lived among them at one time, gratifying the cravings of our flesh and following its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature deserving of wrath. <sup>4</sup>But because of his great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, <sup>5</sup>made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in transgressions – it is by grace you have been saved.
<sup>15</sup>And having disarmed the powers and authorities, he made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.

<sup>14</sup>Since the children have flesh and blood, he too shared in their humanity so that by his death he might break the power of him who holds the power of death – that is, the devil – <sup>15</sup>and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death.

elements.question: What do these passages say Christ has achieved against the powers of evil, and by what means?
elements.sampleAnswer: Ephesians says we were dead in our sins, following the ruler of the kingdom of the air, but God, rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ. Colossians says Christ disarmed the powers and authorities and triumphed over them by the cross. Hebrews says Christ shared in our humanity so that by his death he might break the power of the devil, who holds the power of death, and free those held in slavery by the fear of death. In each case Christ’s death and what it achieved is the means of victory.
elements.questionHint: In each passage look for what Christ did and how he did it.

elements.text: How does Satan attack Christians?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.

elements.question: Who led Jesus into the wilderness, and for what purpose? What does this show about one way Satan attacks?
elements.sampleAnswer: The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. This shows that the devil attacks by tempting people, even those who are following God. Jesus himself was tempted, and so believers should expect temptation too.
elements.questionHint: Notice both who led Jesus there and who did the tempting.

elements.text: How does Satan attack unbelievers?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup>The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that they cannot see the light of the gospel that displays the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

elements.question: What does Paul say the ‘god of this age’ has done to unbelievers, and what can they not see?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers. As a result they cannot see the light of the gospel, which displays the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. This shows that the devil attacks unbelievers by keeping them from seeing the truth about Jesus.
elements.questionHint: Look at what has been done to the mind and what that prevents people from seeing.

elements.text: How should Christians respond to Satan?

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup>Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
<sup>9</sup>Resist him, standing firm in the faith, because you know that the family of believers throughout the world is undergoing the same kind of sufferings.
<sup>11</sup>Put on the full armour of God, so that you can take your stand against the devil’s schemes.

elements.question: What are Christians told to do about the devil in these verses, and what does James promise?
elements.sampleAnswer: James says to submit to God and to resist the devil, and he promises that the devil will flee. Peter says to resist him by standing firm in the faith, knowing that believers throughout the world are undergoing the same sufferings. Paul says to put on the full armour of God so that we can take our stand against the devil’s schemes.
elements.questionHint: Look for the commands: submit, resist, stand firm and put on.

elements.text: What is the armour of God? How is it used?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup>Therefore put on the full armour of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you may be able to stand your ground, and after you have done everything, to stand. <sup>14</sup>Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled round your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness in place, <sup>15</sup>and with your feet fitted with the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace. <sup>16</sup>In addition to all this, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. <sup>17</sup>Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. <sup>18</sup>And pray in the Spirit on all occasions with all kinds of prayers and requests. With this in mind, be alert and always keep on praying for all the Lord’s people.

elements.question: List the pieces of armour Paul names and what each one is. What does he say about prayer, and what is the armour for?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul names the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, feet fitted with the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. The shield can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. The armour is put on so that when the day of evil comes, we can stand our ground. Paul ends by urging prayer in the Spirit on all occasions, being alert and praying for all the Lord’s people.
elements.questionHint: Work through verses 14 to 17 piece by piece, then read verse 18.

elements.text: What will happen to the devil in the end?

elements.passageText: <sup>41</sup>‘Then he will say to those on his left, “Depart from me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

<sup>10</sup>And the devil, who deceived them, was thrown into the lake of burning sulphur, where the beast and the false prophet had been thrown. They will be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

elements.question: What do these verses say about the devil’s final destiny?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus speaks of the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. In Revelation the devil, who deceived people, is thrown into the lake of burning sulphur, where the beast and the false prophet had been thrown. There they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever. The devil’s end is certain.
elements.questionHint: Compare what Jesus says has been ‘prepared’ for the devil with what happens to him in Revelation.

elements.text: Key truths

For Christians, Satan is a very real and active enemy and we must take him seriously.

“Be alert and of sober mind. Your enemy the devil prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour.” — 1 Peter 5:8

We must submit to God’s authority if we are to stand firm against Satan.

“Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” — James 4:7
To think about

elements.question: Can you think of a situation when you were aware of being under attack by Satan? Were you able to resist his attack?
How can you prepare yourself against Satan’s attacks? Read Ephesians 6:13-18.

elements.text: Think of a family waiting for someone to come home after a long time away. The waiting shapes how they live: what they prepare and what they look forward to. Because of his resurrection, Jesus has already won the victory over sin, evil and death. But he will not be universally acknowledged as King until he returns to earth, and then he will bring in a whole new creation, restored, redeemed and healed. In this study we look at the warnings we are given while we wait, how we know he will come again, what will happen, and how this should affect our lives now.
During these ‘last days’, what warnings are we given as we wait for Jesus to return?

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup>Dear children, this is the last hour; and as you have heard that the antichrist is coming, even now many antichrists have come. This is how we know it is the last hour. <sup>19</sup>They went out from us, but they did not really belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us; but their going showed that none of them belonged to us. <sup>20</sup>But you have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth. <sup>21</sup>I do not write to you because you do not know the truth, but because you do know it and because no lie comes from the truth. <sup>22</sup>Who is the liar? It is whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ. Such a person is the antichrist – denying the Father and the Son. <sup>23</sup>No one who denies the Son has the Father; whoever acknowledges the Son has the Father also. <sup>24</sup>As for you, see that what you have heard from the beginning remains in you. If it does, you also will remain in the Son and in the Father. <sup>25</sup>And this is what he promised us – eternal life. <sup>26</sup>I am writing these things to you about those who are trying to lead you astray.

<sup>1</sup>Dear friends, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. <sup>2</sup>This is how you can recognise the Spirit of God: every spirit that acknowledges that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, <sup>3</sup>but every spirit that does not acknowledge Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming and even now is already in the world.

elements.question: What does John say about the ‘last hour’ and about antichrists? How does he tell believers to recognise teaching that is not from God?
elements.sampleAnswer: John says it is the last hour and that many antichrists have come. The antichrist is whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ, and so denies the Father and the Son. He tells believers to see that what they heard from the beginning remains in them, and to test the spirits to see whether they are from God. A spirit that acknowledges that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, but one that does not is not.
elements.questionHint: Look at what John says antichrists deny, and at how he tells his readers to test every spirit.

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting the one who called you to live in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel – <sup>7</sup>which is really no gospel at all. Evidently some people are throwing you into confusion and are trying to pervert the gospel of Christ. <sup>8</sup>But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel other than the one we preached to you, let them be under God’s curse! <sup>9</sup>As we have already said, so now I say again: if anybody is preaching to you a gospel other than what you accepted, let them be under God’s curse!

elements.question: What is Paul astonished by, and how seriously does he treat preaching a different gospel?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul is astonished that the Galatians are so quickly deserting the one who called them and turning to a different gospel, which is really no gospel at all. Some people are trying to pervert the gospel of Christ. He says that anyone, even an angel from heaven or Paul himself, who preaches a different gospel is to be under God’s curse, and he repeats this in verse 9.
elements.questionHint: Notice that Paul says the same thing twice to make his point.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>But mark this: there will be terrible times in the last days. <sup>2</sup>People will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, proud, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, <sup>3</sup>without love, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, not lovers of the good, <sup>4</sup>treacherous, rash, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God – <sup>5</sup>having a form of godliness but denying its power. Have nothing to do with such people. <sup>6</sup>They are the kind who worm their way into homes and gain control over gullible women, who are loaded down with sins and are swayed by all kinds of evil desires, <sup>7</sup>always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth. <sup>8</sup>Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these teachers oppose the truth. They are men of depraved minds, who, as far as the faith is concerned, are rejected. <sup>9</sup>But they will not get very far because, as in the case of those men, their folly will be clear to everyone.

elements.question: How does Paul describe people in the last days, and what instruction does he give?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says there will be terrible times in the last days. People will be lovers of themselves, of money and of pleasure rather than lovers of God. They will be boastful, proud, ungrateful and without love, having a form of godliness but denying its power. Paul’s instruction is to have nothing to do with such people, and he says that their folly will be clear to everyone.
elements.questionHint: Look for the phrase ‘a form of godliness’ in verse 5 and for what Paul says to do about such people.
keyTerms: lovers of themselves|lovers of money|lovers of pleasure

elements.question: What do you think the Bible means by ‘the last days’?
elements.answer: Many people use ‘the last days’ for a short period just before Jesus returns. In these passages, John writes ‘this is the last hour’ in his own day, and the book speaks of ‘these last days’ as the time in which we wait for Jesus to return. It is a time when Jesus has already won the victory but is not yet acknowledged as King, and the warnings in these passages apply to the whole of it.

elements.text: How do we know Jesus will come again?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup>‘In my vision at night I looked, and there before me was one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into his presence. <sup>14</sup>He was given authority, glory and sovereign power; all nations and peoples of every language worshipped him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and his kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.

elements.question: What does Daniel see, and what is given to the one he sees?
elements.sampleAnswer: Daniel sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approaches the Ancient of Days and is given authority, glory and sovereign power. All nations and peoples of every language worship him. His dominion is everlasting and his kingdom will never be destroyed.
elements.questionHint: Notice what the figure is coming with and what he receives.

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup>My Father’s house has many rooms; if that were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? <sup>3</sup>And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and take you to be with me that you also may be where I am.

elements.question: What does Jesus promise in these verses?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus says his Father’s house has many rooms and that he is going to prepare a place for his followers. He promises that he will come back and take them to be with him, so that they may also be where he is. The purpose of his return is to bring his followers into his own presence.
elements.questionHint: Look for what Jesus says he is going to do and what he will do afterwards.

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup>They were looking intently up into the sky as he was going, when suddenly two men dressed in white stood beside them. <sup>11</sup>‘Men of Galilee,’ they said, ‘why do you stand here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen him go into heaven.’

elements.question: What do the two men say to the disciples as they watch Jesus go, and what do they promise?
elements.sampleAnswer: The two men in white ask the disciples why they stand looking into the sky. They say that this same Jesus, who has been taken from them into heaven, will come back in the same way they have seen him go. The promise is that Jesus himself will return.
elements.questionHint: Notice the way Jesus left and the way the men say he will return.

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup>‘Look, he is coming with the clouds,’ and ‘every eye will see him, even those who pierced him’; and all peoples on earth ‘will mourn because of him.’ So shall it be! Amen.

elements.question: How does John describe Jesus’ coming, and who will see it?
elements.sampleAnswer: John says that Jesus is coming with the clouds and that every eye will see him, even those who pierced him. All peoples on earth will mourn because of him. His coming will therefore be seen by everyone and not just by his followers.
elements.questionHint: Look at what accompanies him and at who is included in ‘every eye’.

elements.text: What do we know about His Second Coming?

elements.passageText: <sup>44</sup>So you also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour when you do not expect him.
<sup>10</sup>But the day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar; the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and everything done in it will be laid bare.

elements.question: What do these verses say about when and how Jesus will return?
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus says the Son of Man will come at an hour when we do not expect him, so we must be ready. Peter says the day of the Lord will come like a thief. On that day the heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and everything done in it will be laid bare. The time is unknown, and so we are to be ready.
elements.questionHint: Look at the two comparisons: an hour you do not expect, and a thief.

elements.text: What will happen when Jesus comes back?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup>For the Lord himself will come down from heaven, with a loud command, with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet call of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first. <sup>17</sup>After that, we who are still alive and are left will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will be with the Lord for ever.
<sup>2</sup>Dear friends, now we are children of God, and what we will be has not yet been made known. But we know that when Christ appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is.

elements.question: What will happen to believers, both dead and living, when the Lord comes? What will we be like?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says the Lord himself will come down from heaven with a loud command, the voice of the archangel and the trumpet call of God. The dead in Christ will rise first, and then those who are still alive will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. So we will be with the Lord for ever. John adds that when Christ appears we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is.
elements.questionHint: Follow the order in 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17: who rises first, and what happens next?

elements.text: What will happen to those who reject Him?

elements.passageText: <sup>31</sup>‘When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, he will sit on his glorious throne. <sup>32</sup>All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate the people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. <sup>33</sup>He will put the sheep on his right and the goats on his left. <sup>34</sup>‘Then the King will say to those on his right, “Come, you who are blessed by my Father; take your inheritance, the kingdom prepared for you since the creation of the world. <sup>35</sup>For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you invited me in, <sup>36</sup>I needed clothes and you clothed me, I was ill and you looked after me, I was in prison and you came to visit me.” <sup>37</sup>‘Then the righteous will answer him, “Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you something to drink? <sup>38</sup>When did we see you a stranger and invite you in, or needing clothes and clothe you? <sup>39</sup>When did we see you ill or in prison and go to visit you?” <sup>40</sup>‘The King will reply, “Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.” <sup>41</sup>‘Then he will say to those on his left, “Depart from me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. <sup>42</sup>For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink, <sup>43</sup>I was a stranger and you did not invite me in, I needed clothes and you did not clothe me, I was ill and in prison and you did not look after me.” <sup>44</sup>‘They also will answer, “Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or needing clothes or ill or in prison, and did not help you?” <sup>45</sup>‘He will reply, “Truly I tell you, whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for me.” <sup>46</sup>‘Then they will go away to eternal punishment, but the righteous to eternal life.’

elements.question: When the Son of Man comes in his glory, how are people separated, and what does each group receive? What does Jesus say about what they did or did not do?
elements.sampleAnswer: The Son of Man sits on his glorious throne and separates the people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Those on his right are invited to take their inheritance in the kingdom prepared for them. Those on his left are told to depart into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. What they did or did not do for the least of Jesus’ brothers and sisters counts as done or not done for him, and they go to eternal punishment but the righteous to eternal life.
elements.questionHint: Notice what the Son of Man says the two groups did or did not do, and the words used for each outcome.

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup>and give relief to you who are troubled, and to us as well. This will happen when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven in blazing fire with his powerful angels. <sup>8</sup>He will punish those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus. <sup>9</sup>They will be punished with everlasting destruction and shut out from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might

elements.question: What does Paul say will happen when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven, and what will happen to those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel?
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven in blazing fire with his powerful angels, he will give relief to those who are troubled. He will punish those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel. They will be punished with everlasting destruction and shut out from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might.
elements.questionHint: Notice both the relief promised to the troubled and the punishment of the others.

elements.text: What will the New Heavens and New Earth be like?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and there was no longer any sea. <sup>2</sup>I saw the Holy City, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband. <sup>3</sup>And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, ‘Look! God’s dwelling-place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. <sup>4</sup>“He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death” or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.’

elements.question: What does John see, and what does he hear? What will no longer exist?
elements.sampleAnswer: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, because the first heaven and earth have passed away. He sees the Holy City, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God. A loud voice says that God’s dwelling-place is now among the people, and that he will dwell with them and be their God. God will wipe every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain.
elements.questionHint: Look for what is new, what God does, and what there will be ‘no more’ of.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb <sup>2</sup>down the middle of the great street of the city. On each side of the river stood the tree of life, bearing twelve crops of fruit, yielding its fruit every month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. <sup>3</sup>No longer will there be any curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in the city, and his servants will serve him. <sup>4</sup>They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. <sup>5</sup>There will be no more night. They will not need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, for the Lord God will give them light. And they will reign for ever and ever.

elements.question: What does John see in the city, and what will God’s servants do? What will no longer be there?
elements.sampleAnswer: John sees the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on each side, whose leaves are for the healing of the nations. There will be no longer any curse, and there will be no more night, because the Lord God will give them light. His servants will serve him, see his face and reign for ever and ever.
elements.questionHint: Notice what is there, such as the river, the tree and the throne, and what is absent, such as the curse and the night.

elements.text: How should Jesus’ coming again affect our daily lives?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup>For the grace of God has appeared that offers salvation to all people. <sup>12</sup>It teaches us to say ‘No’ to ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in this present age, <sup>13</sup>while we wait for the blessed hope – the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ, <sup>14</sup>who gave himself for us to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify for himself a people that are his very own, eager to do what is good.

elements.question: What does the grace of God teach us to say ‘No’ to, and how should we live while we wait? What has Christ done, and what does he want for his people?
elements.sampleAnswer: The grace of God teaches us to say ‘No’ to ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in this present age. We do this while we wait for the blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ. Christ gave himself for us to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify for himself a people who are eager to do what is good.
elements.questionHint: Notice that grace is pictured as a teacher: look for what it teaches.

elements.text: Key truths

In the world in which there is so much pain and suffering, Christians can look forward with great joy to the return of Jesus.

“But our citizenship is in heaven. And we eagerly await a Saviour from there, the Lord Jesus Christ,...” — Philippians 3:20

We must be ready for Jesus’ return: He might come at any time.

“So you also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour when you do not expect him.” — Matthew 24:44
To think about

elements.question: Are you looking forward to Jesus coming again? Why, or why not?
Knowing that Jesus might return at any time, is there anything in your life that you need to change?

blocks.title: People who follow Jesus
blocks.body: This volume is written for Christians. It assumes that you have already put your trust in Jesus, and it looks at what living as a Christian involves: being sure of your salvation, the cost of following Jesus, the Bible, prayer, the Church, worship and service, Satan, and Jesus’ return.

blocks.title: People new to the faith
blocks.body: If you have only recently become a Christian, these studies will help you build solid foundations for the Christian life. If you are not yet sure what it means to become a Christian, you may want to start with volume 1, and in particular with its last chapter, ‘Knowing the Bible, Knowing God’.

blocks.title: People who have been Christians for some time
blocks.body: These studies are also a helpful refresher for those who have followed Jesus for years and want to review the basics of their faith. You may be surprised by what you learn.

blocks.title: People discipling others
blocks.body: If you are walking alongside someone else in their faith, as a mentor, a small group leader or a friend, this volume gives you a structured way to work through the basics of Christian living together. Each chapter ends with personal reflection questions that naturally prompt deeper conversation.

blocks.title: On your own
blocks.body: This study works well as a personal study. Work through each chapter at your own pace, read the Bible passages, write your answers to the questions, and think about the reflection questions at the end. Allow about an hour for each study, though some chapters may take longer if a question stops you in your tracks.

blocks.title: In a group
blocks.body: The study also works well in a small group. Ideally, each person works through the chapter individually first and writes their answers, and then the group meets to compare answers and discuss. A possible pattern for a session is about 35 minutes reviewing the answers to the Bible questions, about 15 minutes on the Key truths, and about 20 minutes on the reflection questions. A leader could run the eight studies in this volume as an eight-week course.

blocks.title: Working with a leader or mentor
blocks.body:
It can make a real difference to have someone guiding you through the study: a group leader, a pastor, or a more experienced Christian who can help you think through your answers and questions. Perhaps they are the one who recommended this study to you in the first place.

At the end of each chapter, the Share button lets you send your written answers directly to your leader or mentor, via WhatsApp, email, or any other app on your phone. This gives them a window into your thinking before you meet, and makes for much richer conversation.

blocks.title: Pray
blocks.body: Before you start each study, ask God to help you understand what he is saying in the Bible verses. After you have finished, ask him to show you how he wants you to put into practice what you have learned, and to help you do it.

blocks.title: Form your own view first
blocks.body: As you consider each question, it is a good idea to come to your own view on the answer before you tap ⓘ to read the Bible passage.

blocks.title: Two kinds of questions
blocks.body: Each chapter has two kinds of questions. The Bible questions are tied to specific passages, asking you to look carefully at what the text says. The reflection questions at the end are more personal, asking what the chapter means for you specifically.

blocks.title: Common Misunderstanding boxes
blocks.body: Throughout the study you will meet cards headed Common Misunderstanding. These address words, like church, worship or the last days, that Christians use all the time but that are often misunderstood. Take a moment to think about what you understand by the word, then tap Find out to see a short clarification.

blocks.title: Key truths
blocks.body: At the end of each Bible section you will find two Key truths: short statements, each with the Bible verse it rests on. They sum up what the study has shown.

leadersNotesData.subtitle: Truth Unlocked: Christian Living
intro: These notes are designed to help group leaders and mentors get the most out of each chapter – both for the people they are leading and for themselves. They are not a substitute for working through the material yourself first. The best leaders are those who have worked through the questions personally before they help others doing the same.

Create a safe space for honesty. The questions in this study are designed to prompt real reflection, not just correct answers. Your job is to make the group feel safe enough to say what they actually think, not what they think a Christian is supposed to say.
Don’t rush the silences. Some of the best moments in a group study happen after a question lands and nobody speaks for a few seconds. Resist the urge to fill every silence.
Watch for the person who goes quiet. Sometimes the most significant thing happening in the room is with the person who says the least. Check in with them afterwards.

keyPoints.body:
This study asks how we can be certain that we are truly saved. The key movements are (1) God wants believers to know (1 John 5:13), (2) the promises of Jesus (John 1:12; 6:47; 10:27–28; Revelation 3:20), (3) the Spirit’s witness that we are God’s children (Romans 8:16), (4) Jesus’ constant presence and God’s ability to keep believers (Matthew 28:20; Jude 24; Romans 8:31–39), and (5) what to do when we sin: confess it (1 John 1:9).

The book’s key truth is that when we sin we do not lose our salvation, but we do need to confess our sin, because unconfessed sin clouds our relationship with God. The questions ask only what the passages say, so there is no need to press the point further than the passages do.

pastorals.body:
Reflection question 1 invites honesty about doubt. Some in the group may doubt because of failure or because of how they feel, so take whatever is said seriously and avoid quick reassurance.

Revelation 3:20 was written to a church (in Laodicea). The book uses it as a general picture of Jesus’ welcome. If someone raises the context, acknowledge it.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who treat certainty as a feeling. The study points to God’s promises, not to how we feel on a particular day. Also watch for anyone who hears assurance as permission to carry on sinning: the study shows that sin matters, which is why we confess it.

keyPoints.body:
Salvation is a free gift, but living as a Christian has a real cost. The study looks at what that means (Romans 12:1–2; Matthew 5:13–16), what we give up (Hebrews 12:1; Colossians 3:5–11), what we take on (Philippians 2:1–5; Colossians 4:2; Hebrews 10:24–25; 2 Corinthians 8–9; Acts 17:11), the opposition the early Christians faced, and how to respond to suffering (John 16:33; 1 Peter 4:12–16).

The final reflection question asks the group to look again at what the cross cost Jesus (Philippians 2:6–8).

pastorals.body:
Some in the group may be suffering for their faith, or may have lost relationships or opportunities because of it. Reflection questions 1 and 2 touch on this directly, so allow people to speak, or to pass, as they prefer.

The key truth quotes Luke 14:26–27, a hard saying. The questions do not explain it, so it is best to let the text stand and to point to how seriously Jesus takes following him.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who hear ‘cost’ as the price of being saved, or who conclude that Christians who are not suffering cannot be real Christians. The study says salvation is a free gift, and that the cost is the cost of discipleship. Watch too for those who hear the two lists in Colossians 3 as a list of rules: Paul gives the reason that believers have put on the new self.

keyPoints.body:
The Bible mattered to Jesus (Luke 4:1–13). It was given so that we may believe and be equipped (John 20:31; 2 Timothy 3:15–17), and it came from God through human writers carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:19–21). The Bereans show how to study it (Acts 17:11–12). We should expect light, joy and growth from it (Psalm 119:105; Jeremiah 15:16), and we are to respond by doing what it says, relying on it and storing it up (James 1:22–25; Acts 20:32; Psalm 119:11).

The book describes Scripture as God-breathed, with God himself inspiring and directing the writing. It does not go further than that, and neither do the questions.

pastorals.body:
Many people find regular Bible reading hard. Reflection question 1 invites practical suggestions: a fixed time of day, a reading plan, or a friend to read alongside. Take care not to make anyone feel guilty.

Some people read the Bible and never sense that God is speaking. Reflection question 2 is worth taking slowly.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who treat Bible reading as an achievement, or who read without ever acting on it (James 1:22). If someone raises questions about how the Bible came to be, or about difficult passages, note them and return to them later rather than letting them take over the session.

keyPoints.body: Prayer mattered to Jesus (Matthew 14:23; Mark 1:35; Luke 6:12). The study shows what prayer involves: confession, thanksgiving, requests, and praying for others and asking others to pray for us (Psalm 32:5; Philippians 4:6–7; Romans 15:30; Colossians 1:9; Ephesians 1:16–17). It then looks at instructions about praying (Matthew 6:6; Hebrews 4:16; Luke 18:1–8; 1 Thessalonians 5:17), what Paul prayed for others, why prayers may not be answered as we wish (2 Corinthians 12:7–9; James 4:3), and how the Holy Spirit helps us (Romans 8:26).

pastorals.body: Unanswered prayer can be painful. Someone in the group may have prayed for healing or for a loved one and not seen the answer they hoped for. The two passages in this study give two reasons without suggesting that every unanswered prayer is explained by them. Be careful never to imply that a person’s loss is due to wrong motives or to lack of faith.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who treat prayer as a technique, or who feel they pray badly. Romans 8:26 is written for them. Reflection question 2 invites people to pray with others, so you may want to finish the session with a time of prayer together.

keyPoints.body: The Church is God’s people, not a building. It is described as a body, a household and a holy nation (1 Corinthians 12; Ephesians 2:19–20; 1 Peter 2:9–10), and Christ is its head (Ephesians 5:23). Its purpose is to bear witness to Jesus across the world (Acts 1:8; 1 Peter 2:9). Christians meet together (Luke 4:16; Acts 2:42; Hebrews 10:24–25) to carry one another’s burdens, to value every member and to grow together (Galatians 6:1–2; 1 Corinthians 12:21–27; Ephesians 4:14–16).

pastorals.body:
Some in the group may have been hurt by a church, or may not currently belong to one. Reflection question 1 asks about their own involvement, so be gentle, and encourage people to connect with a local church.

Ephesians 5:23 and 5:25–27 are written in the context of marriage. The questions ask only about Christ and the church, so try not to let the session turn into a discussion about marriage.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for ‘the church’ being spoken of as ‘them’, as if it meant the building or the leaders, rather than ‘us’. Watch too for people who attend but are not involved, and for anyone who feels that they have nothing to contribute: 1 Corinthians 12 says that every part is needed.

keyPoints.body: True worship is the surrender of the whole of our lives to God (Romans 12:1–2). Jesus served with humility and love, washing his disciples’ feet (John 13:1–16), and we are to come with thanksgiving and in spirit and truth (Psalm 100:4; John 4:23–24). We are to love one another and do good to all (John 13:34–35; Galatians 6:10), to serve God in our work (Colossians 3:22–25; Titus 2:9–10) and to witness (Matthew 28:19–20; 2 Peter 3:9; Matthew 5:13–16; Mark 5:19–20; 1 Peter 3:15).

pastorals.body:
Question 6 uses passages written to slaves in the ancient world. They are not an endorsement of slavery: they show how believers living under very unjust conditions were to work, and whom they were really serving. Handle the passage with care, because someone in the group may have experienced exploitation at work.

Reflection question 3 (Martha and Mary) can bring out strong views. Invite them without settling the answer for the group.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who hear ‘serve’ as ‘do more’ and feel guilty. The study starts from God’s mercy (Romans 12:1), and the reflection question about serving out of duty is there to help people notice the difference. Watch too for anyone who thinks worship only means music.

keyPoints.body:
Satan is a real and active enemy. The study looks at how he is described (John 8:44; 2 Corinthians 11:14–15; Matthew 13:19; 1 Peter 5:8), how Jesus defeated him (Ephesians 2:1–5; Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15), how he attacks Christians and unbelievers (Matthew 4:1; 2 Corinthians 4:4), how Christians should respond (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:9; Ephesians 6:11–18), and what will happen to him in the end (Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:10).

The study’s introduction states that Satan was once a heavenly being whose pride and ambition led to his fall. This is the book’s teaching and is not shown by the passages in this study, so no question asks about it.

pastorals.body: Reflection question 1 invites people to describe a time when they felt under attack. Some may be afraid, may have had involvement in the occult, or may have had frightening experiences. Keep the discussion pastoral and calm, and reassure the group with Jesus’ victory (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15). Offer to talk with anyone individually afterwards.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for two extremes: dismissing the devil as a joke, and seeing him behind everything that goes wrong. The study’s emphasis is on submitting to God and standing firm, rather than on Satan himself.

keyPoints.body: While we wait for Jesus to return we are warned against false teaching and against the attitudes of the last days (1 John 2:18–26; 4:1–3; Galatians 1:6–9; 2 Timothy 3:1–9). Scripture promises that he will come again (Daniel 7:13–14; John 14:2–3; Acts 1:10–11; Revelation 1:7), and that the time is unexpected (Matthew 24:44; 2 Peter 3:10). The study looks at what will happen when he returns, what will happen to those who reject him, and what the new heavens and new earth will be like (Revelation 21:1–4; 22:1–5). It ends by asking how this should affect daily life (Titus 2:11–14).

pastorals.body:
Matthew 25:31–46 and 2 Thessalonians 1:7–9 speak of final punishment. This can be very hard for people who have family or friends who do not follow Jesus. Be honest about what the passages say, but speak gently, and make time for people to respond.

Some people are anxious about the end; others are fascinated by it. Both reactions need care.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for speculation about dates, signs and the order of events. The passages in this study say that Jesus will return, that the time is unexpected, and that we should be ready, so keep the group to that. Christians differ on the details of the last days, and that need not divide the group.

paras: Rick Creighton grew up in Northern Ireland and studied maths at Oxford and then taught maths at a secondary school in England. After that, he studied theology at Moore Theological College in Sydney and London School of Theology.

He served as a church pastor in England for ten years, before moving to Nigeria in 2012, where he has been teaching at ECWA Theological Seminary Kagoro and Jos ECWA Theological Seminary. He has been involved with BeaconLight Training since 2003.
Rick is married to Alanna. They have three children: Asha, Conor, and Jack.

paras: BeaconLight is a non-denominational Christian training organisation based in the UK, founded in 1995. Its aim is to equip Christians worldwide with practically-applied Biblical gospel ministry tools — resources designed to help people both equip themselves and equip others.

BeaconLight’s resources include CrossCheck, which enables Christians to explain their faith and lead others to Jesus, and Word@Work, a verse-by-verse applied devotional commentary of the whole New Testament. BeaconLight also provides printed Biblical resources to prisons, seafarers, police, and the armed services.
BeaconLight believes that Christian ministry should be free of charge, and all its online materials are available without registration or payment. The ministry is funded entirely by donations.
